title: These Birds Carry Burning Sticks to Start New Fires, on Purpose

scenes.text: In northern Australia, some bushfires are spread by birds.
Black kites, whistling kites and brown falcons gather at the edge of grass fires on the savanna, and wait.
Then, witnesses say, a bird swoops down, grabs a smouldering stick in its beak or talons, and flies off with it.
It drops the stick in unburnt grass, sometimes on the far side of a road or river that had stopped the flames.
A new fire starts. Everything hiding in that grass has to run, and the birds are already circling.
Aboriginal people have told of firehawks for thousands of years. Scientists gathered the accounts in 2017. The birds can't light a fire. They just know how to move one.

description:
In the savannas of northern Australia, black kites, whistling kites and brown falcons have been reported picking up burning sticks in their beaks or talons and dropping them in unburnt grass, flushing out prey.
A 2017 paper in the Journal of Ethnobiology gathered Aboriginal knowledge and eyewitness accounts from rangers and firefighters. The evidence so far is testimony, not film, and the birds cannot start a fire themselves.
Tool use, or just a lucky habit?
subject: black kite
first_comment: A 1963 book already described birds dropping burning brands in grass up to half a kilometre away. Do you count this as using a tool?
